An immigrant is a person who comes to live permanently in a country that is not the country they were born in or originally belonged to.

The key word here is permanently — or at least with the intention of staying long-term. An immigrant is not just visiting. They are making a new country their home.

Imagine Maria was born and raised in Mexico. She decides to move to Canada and settle there for good — build a life, find work, maybe raise a family. The moment she arrives in Canada with the intention of staying, she becomes an immigrant in Canada.

That's it at its most basic.
The Two-Sided Nature of the Word

Here is something very important that trips up a lot of learners: the same person can be called two different things depending on which country you're looking at.

Take Maria from the example above.

  • From Canada's point of view, Maria is an immigrant — she came in.
  • From Mexico's point of view, Maria is an emigrant — she went out.

So:

  • Immigrant = someone who enters a new country to live there.
  • Emigrant = someone who leaves their home country to live elsewhere.

Same person. Same journey. Different word based on direction. Think of it like a door — "immigrant" describes walking through the door into the new room, while "emigrant" describes leaving the old room.
What Makes Someone an Immigrant (and Not Something Else)

The word "immigrant" is often confused with similar words. Understanding the differences makes the meaning much sharper.

Immigrant vs. Tourist / Visitor
A tourist comes for a short time — to see places, attend events, or visit people — and then goes back home. An immigrant comes to stay. The intention is what matters. If you come for two weeks, you're a visitor. If you come to build your life there, you're an immigrant.

Immigrant vs. Migrant
A "migrant" (especially a migrant worker) is someone who moves — often repeatedly — from place to place, usually for seasonal or temporary work. They don't necessarily intend to settle down permanently. An immigrant, by contrast, intends to settle. That said, in everyday speech, people sometimes use "migrant" and "immigrant" loosely and interchangeably, but technically they are different.

Immigrant vs. Refugee
A refugee is a specific type of person who is forced to flee their country because of war, persecution, or disaster — they had no safe choice but to leave. An immigrant, in the traditional sense, makes a more voluntary choice to move (for a better job, education, family reasons, lifestyle, etc.). However, a refugee who is officially granted the right to stay in a new country permanently can also legally become an immigrant in that country over time. The words describe different situations, but they can overlap.

Immigrant vs. Expat
An "expat" (short for expatriate) is also someone living outside their home country. In practice, "expat" is used more informally to describe skilled professionals or wealthy individuals who relocate abroad — often temporarily. "Immigrant" tends to be the more formal, legal, and universal term. The honest truth is that the distinction between "expat" and "immigrant" is often cultural and societal rather than strictly legal.

Not all immigrants arrive the same way. Here are the main categories:

Legal / Documented Immigrants
These are people who move to a new country through that country's official process. They have the proper paperwork — a visa, a residency permit, or similar legal status. The new country has officially approved their right to be there.

Undocumented / Unauthorized Immigrants
These are people who live in a country without the legal permission of that country's government. They may have entered without permission, or they may have entered legally (say, on a tourist visa) but stayed after that permission expired. This is a sensitive and often politically charged topic, and different people and governments use different terms for this group.

Economic Immigrants
People who move primarily to find better work, better wages, or better economic opportunities. This is one of the most common reasons people immigrate.

Family-Based Immigrants
People who move to a country because a close family member (spouse, parent, child) is already a citizen or legal resident there, and they are permitted to join them.

Humanitarian Immigrants
People granted the right to stay in a new country for humanitarian reasons — including refugees and asylum seekers who are given legal protection.
The Process: What Happens When Someone Immigrates

When a person immigrates, they typically go through a legal process set by the country they're moving to. This can involve applying for a visa (permission to enter), then a residency permit (permission to stay long-term), and eventually — if they choose and qualify — citizenship (becoming a full legal member of that country). Citizenship is the final step where an immigrant can become a full citizen of their new country, with all the same rights as someone born there.
The Human Reality Behind the Word

It's worth remembering that "immigrant" is not just a legal or political category — it describes real human beings who have left behind their home, their language, their culture, their family, and their familiar surroundings to begin a new life somewhere else. This can be driven by hope, ambition, necessity, love, survival, or a combination of all of these. The word carries immense human weight.

An immigrant is a person who moves to a foreign country with the intention of living there permanently or long-term.

Everything else above is the detail that makes that simple truth fully understood.
